s1_e7904.bin.desc: Epoch 7,904, the first birth I caught. The parent's loop [ , < , } } has no closing ]. The partner's first byte is one, so the loop closes across the seam, 63 passes, and writes a compacted, mirrored replicator.

s25_e7880.bin.desc: Epoch 7,880. The parent's [ … + … < has no ] of its own; it borrows the one at the partner's byte 1. The lineage took over 320 epochs later.

s30_e7710.bin.desc: Epoch 7,710. The parent is a ladder of [·[·[ ending in a { > . > loop body with no ]. The partner's byte-1 ] closes it.

s39_e9994.bin.desc: Epoch 9,994. The partner starts with ]] (armour twice over), and the first of them closes the parent's loop.

s24_e15952.bin.desc: Epoch 15,952. A sparse parent: [ < , and two } scattered over 64 bytes. The ] it borrows sits at the partner's byte 4.

s37_e3996.bin.desc: Epoch 3,996. The same trick with the partner's byte-0 ], but this lineage died within a couple of hundred epochs. About half of all births end like this.

s17_e11179.bin.desc: Epoch 11,179. A borrowed ] at the partner's byte 0 again; the lineage was gone by epoch 11,300.

s18_e101166.bin.desc: Epoch 101,166. No seam loop. The parent opens with < … < ], which tests the partner's byte 126 and halts unless it is zero. This partner ends in 00, so the parent runs and writes a mirrored copy that carries the zero along.

s502_e11048.bin.desc: The other BFF variant: bytes 0 and 1 aim the heads and execution starts at byte 2. The borrowed ] sits deep in the partner (byte 35), and the copy comes out direct, not mirrored.

s504_e39007.bin.desc: No seam loop. The parent runs 8 instructions and writes two , bytes into the newborn, which completes the newborn's own loop [ > , , } ].

s510_e13149.bin.desc: No seam loop, and the newborn is the top row this time. A single byte written during the interaction completes the newborn's loop.
